title: Industries: from manufacturing to service
subtitle: heavy industry, privatisation, piecework, sweatshop
summary: Describe industries and the way they work - heavy and light, high-tech and low-tech, nationalised and privatised - and the practices, good and bad, that go with them.

lesson.heading: Heavy and light, manufacturing and service

left.label: heavy industry / manufacturing industry
left.text: **Heavy industry** means big plants such as steel works and shipbuilding. **Manufacturing industry** makes things, for example consumer goods.
examples: **Heavy industry** has declined in most of western Europe.
We need to encourage **manufacturing industries** that make things we can sell.

right.label: light industry / service industry
right.text: **Light industry** makes smaller items such as car parts and TV sets. **Service industry** serves people - tourism, banking, insurance.
examples: Now we're more dependent on **light industry**.
The economy cannot depend only on **service industries**.

lesson.heading: How advanced is the technology?

left.label: high-technology (high-tech) / cutting-edge technology
left.text: **High-tech** industries involve computers, for example the software industry. **Cutting-edge technology** is new and innovative.
examples: In this area there are a lot of **high-tech** industries.

right.label: low-technology (low-tech) / conventional technology
right.text: **Low-tech** industries involve little or no computer technology. **Conventional technology** is standard and proven.
examples: In the north they depend more on **low-tech** industries.
The company has to rely on **conventional technology**.

lesson.note: High-tech and low-tech are the informal short forms of high-technology and low-technology.

lesson.heading: Who owns industry?
lesson.text: **Nationalisation**, or **state ownership**, is when industry is owned by the government. **Privatisation** is the opposite: selling off state railways, for example, to private companies. Many big industries are now run as **public-private partnerships**, partly state-owned and partly owned by private businesses.

examples.text: **State ownership** is less popular than it was, but the trend towards **privatisation** has slowed down.
The nuclear industry receives a huge **subsidy** from the government.
examples.note: subsidy = money or grants that enable an industry to stay in profit

examples.text: The government tries to encourage **inward investment**.
examples.note: inward investment = investment from foreign companies

lesson.heading: Industrial practices
rows: workers are paid only for the amount they produce
you are employed, but the hours vary and some weeks there is no work and no pay
the employment of children to do adult jobs
having a union that negotiates wages and conditions for the people it represents
a factory where people work very long hours for low wages
training people for new jobs and teaching them new skills

lesson.heading: Cutting costs and moving production
lesson.text: The big **multinationals** - companies with operations in many different countries - often close factories as a **cost-cutting exercise**, then **relocate** and **switch production** to countries where labour is cheaper. In many cases **components**, or parts, for cars are imported and then **assembled**, that is put together, rather than manufactured in the country.

examples.text: Many people now work on **zero hours contracts**, which means they have no job security.
Many cheap electrical goods are produced in **sweatshops** in poorer countries.
**Retraining** and **reskilling** are necessary when an economy is modernised.

lesson.heading: Crime in industry
rows: illegal production of goods using another company's brand name
stealing or destroying a rival company's plans or secrets
publishing or copying a book or work of art without the author's permission
passing illegally earned money through the normal banking system without being caught

lesson.text: Relocate normally moves the offices; switch production moves the manufacturing itself.

exercises.prompt: Match each expression with its opposite.
The economy cannot depend only on restaurants and hotels. We need to encourage ___ industries that make things we can sell.
exercises.explanation: Manufacturing industry makes things; service industry serves people.

exercises.prompt: The latest, innovative ___ technology is very expensive, so the company relies on conventional technology.
exercises.hint: (two words with a hyphen: newest and most innovative)
exercises.explanation: Cutting-edge technology is new and innovative; conventional technology is standard and proven.

exercises.prompt: State ownership is less popular than it was, but the trend towards ___ has slowed down.
exercises.explanation: Privatisation is the selling off of state industries to private companies.

exercises.prompt: The nuclear industry receives a huge ___ from the government.
exercises.hint: (money that keeps an industry in profit)
exercises.explanation: A subsidy is a government grant that enables a loss-making industry to continue.

exercises.prompt: Most of the factory workers are on ___ , so they are paid only for what they produce.
exercises.explanation: On piecework, employees are paid only for the amount they produce.

exercises.prompt: The government tries to encourage ___ investment - investment by foreign companies.
exercises.explanation: Inward investment is investment in a country by foreign companies.

exercises.prompt: Many cheap electrical goods are produced in ___ , where people work very long hours for low wages.
exercises.explanation: A sweatshop is a factory where people work very long hours for low wages.

exercises.prompt: What is a zero hours contract?
options: you are employed, but the hours vary and some weeks there is no work and no pay
a contract that guarantees you a fixed number of hours every week
a contract with no fixed end date
a contract that pays you only for what you produce
exercises.explanation: Zero hours contracts give no job security: the number of hours may vary, and some weeks there may be no work at all.

exercises.prompt: 'The company closed two factories as a cost-cutting exercise and switched production abroad.' What does switch production mean?
options: move the centre of manufacturing to a different place
sell the factories to the government
put the parts together in a different order
exercises.explanation: To switch production is to move manufacturing somewhere else, usually where labour is cheaper.

exercises.prompt: Match each problem in industry with the situation that illustrates it.

pairs.right: factories producing illegal copies of top brand names
designs for a new aircraft photographed and sold to a rival
illegal editions of a book, so the author receives no payment
money from the drugs trade passed through ordinary banks
secret trade in untaxed luxury cars

exercises.statement: Reskilling means employing children to do adult jobs.
exercises.explanation: Reskilling is teaching workers new skills; employing children to do adult jobs is child labour.

exercises.prompt: Is each one an example of manufacturing industry or of service industry?
